content: Didanosine is a synthetic nucleoside analogue of the naturally occurring nucleoside deoxyadenosine. In this analogue, the 3′-hydroxyl group of deoxyadenosine is replaced by a hydrogen atom. Once inside cells, didanosine undergoes conversion by cellular enzymes into its active metabolite, dideoxyadenosine 5′-triphosphate. This active metabolite exerts its antiviral effects by inhibiting the activity of HIV-1 reverse transcriptase. It achieves this inhibition through two mechanisms: first, by competing with the natural substrate, deoxyadenosine 5′-triphosphate, and second, by being incorporated into the viral DNA, which results in the termination of viral DNA chain elongation. The anti-HIV-1 activity of didanosine has been studied in various HIV-1-infected lymphoblastic cell lines and monocyte/macrophage cell cultures. In monocyte/macrophage cell cultures, the effective concentration was determined to be 1 µM. HIV-1 isolates with reduced sensitivity to didanosine have been identified both in cell culture and in patients treated with didanosine. Genetic analysis of these isolates from didanosine-treated patients revealed mutations in the reverse transcriptase gene. These mutations led to specific amino acid substitutions, including K65R, L74V, and M184V. Among these, the L74V substitution was the most frequently observed in clinical isolates. Phenotypic analysis of HIV-1 isolates from 60 patients who received didanosine monotherapy for 6 to 24 months (some of whom had prior zidovudine treatment) demonstrated that isolates from 10 of these patients exhibited an average 10-fold reduction in susceptibility to didanosine in cell culture compared to baseline isolates. Clinical isolates with reduced susceptibility to didanosine were found to harbor one or more didanosine resistance-associated substitutions. Cross-resistance has also been observed. HIV-1 isolates from 2 out of 39 patients who received combination therapy with didanosine and zidovudine for up to 2 years exhibited decreased susceptibility to didanosine, lamivudine, stavudine, zalcitabine, and zidovudine in cell culture. These isolates contained five specific substitutions (A62V, V75I, F77L, F116Y, and Q151M) in the reverse transcriptase gene. Additionally, clinical data indicate that the presence of thymidine analogue mutations (M41L, D67N, L210W, T215Y, K219Q) is associated with a reduced response to didanosine.
